Description: Bronze prutahs and half-prutahs (lepta) of Herod the Great, struck at the Jerusalem mint during his reign (king from 37 BC; ruled 40-4 BC). The most common type pairs an anchor inscribed 'of King Herod' in Greek with a double cornucopia and caduceus (Meshorer TJC 59; struck in huge quantities, c. 21-12 BC). Other types include a cornucopia with an eagle — the first coin by a Jewish ruler to carry a graven image, linked to the golden eagle Herod set over the Temple gate c. 4 BC — and an anchor with a galley, possibly recalling the harbor at Caesarea Maritima (built 22-10 BC).
Interpretations: The coins name 'King Herod' — the Matthew 2 ruler — in Greek. Their symbolism is debated: some read the anchor and cornucopiae as continuing Hasmonean types, others as pagan or sovereignty imagery, so do not overclaim a single reading. The eagle type's connection to the Temple-gate eagle is a plausible link, not a certainty. The coinage as a whole shows a ruler balancing Jewish sensibilities (no portraits) with Hellenistic royal imagery.
BiblicalSignificance: Matthew 2 opens 'in the days of Herod the king'; these are the coins of that king, struck in Jerusalem in the years around Jesus' birth, and they name him directly.
CurrentLocation: Examples in the Israel Museum and the British Museum
